tool.name: NGINX
tool.tagline: High-performance web server, reverse proxy, load balancer and cache
tool.description: NGINX is a web server: the program that answers browsers' requests. It serves files, handles HTTPS and passes requests on to application servers, and it sits in front of a large share of the world's websites. Knowing how to configure it is a core skill for putting any web application online.

glossary.def: One setting in an NGINX configuration file: a name, its values and a semicolon, like worker_processes auto;. Some hold other settings inside braces.
An NGINX setting that holds other settings inside braces, such as http { ... } or server { ... }.
In NGINX, one of the braced blocks of the configuration (main, events, http, server, location...). Each setting is allowed only in certain ones and applies inside them.
In NGINX, settings flowing down from an outer block to the blocks inside it, unless an inner block sets its own value.
In NGINX, the part of a request's address after the site name: the path, such as /images/cat.png, plus any query string.
In NGINX, the file sent when a request asks for a folder (an address ending in /), usually index.html.
In NGINX, a part of the program that adds a group of features, such as compression or rate limiting. Most come built in; others must be added when NGINX is built.
The program that runs a website's own code (in Python, Java, JavaScript...) and builds its pages and answers, usually sitting behind a web server like NGINX.
Handling a site's HTTPS encryption at the front server (such as NGINX), which then talks plain HTTP to the applications behind it.
The one NGINX process that reads the configuration and starts, watches and replaces the worker processes; it doesn't answer requests itself.
Applying a new configuration without dropping visitors: new worker processes start, old ones finish their current requests and then exit.
A server { } section of NGINX configuration describing one website: which address and port it listens on and which names it answers to.
A location { } section inside a server block holding settings for requests whose path matches it, such as everything under /images/.
The request header naming the site the browser asked for, such as www.example.com; it lets many sites share one IP address.
The server block NGINX uses for a request whose site name matches none of its server blocks: the one marked default_server, or else the first one.
A name under another domain name, such as shop.example.com under example.com.
In NGINX, the servers behind it that requests are passed on to; also the upstream { } block that names a group of them.
A newer version of HTTP that carries many requests and responses at the same time over one connection, making pages load faster.
A response header telling browsers to use only HTTPS for a site for a set time, even if someone types or links plain http://.
A free, automated certificate authority. Its tool certbot proves you control a site, fetches certificates and renews them before they expire.
The usual program for getting free HTTPS certificates from Let's Encrypt and renewing them automatically; it can also edit NGINX settings.
Spreading requests by giving each server a turn in order: first, second, third, then the first again.
NGINX noticing that a backend fails on real requests and skipping it for a while, rather than sending test requests of its own.
Keeping a network connection open after a request so the next request can reuse it, instead of setting up a new connection each time.
A text file of usernames and scrambled (hashed) passwords that a web server checks for basic password protection.
A request NGINX makes internally while handling another, for example to ask a login service whether the visitor may proceed.
A trick where a site shows yours inside an invisible frame and gets visitors to click buttons on it without knowing.
Many requests for the same missing or expired item all reaching the backend at once, which can overload it.
A rate-limiting method: requests fill a bucket that drains at a fixed speed; when it's full, extra requests are turned away.
An HTTP header that only applies to one connection, such as Connection or Upgrade, so a proxy doesn't pass it on by default.
NGINX collecting a backend's response before sending it to the client, freeing the backend quickly but delaying responses meant to stream.
Replacing the NGINX program with a new version while it runs: a new master starts beside the old one, so no connection is lost.
One of the fixed steps NGINX takes every request through (rewrite, access checks, content, logging); each setting runs in its own step, whatever its place in the file.
The paid edition of NGINX from F5, with extra features such as active health checks and a management API.

concepts.name: What NGINX does
concepts.summary: What NGINX is for: serving files, passing requests to your app as a reverse proxy, spreading load and handling HTTPS.
concepts.why: Almost every live website has NGINX or something like it in front; knowing its jobs tells you what to configure there.
concepts.body:
When you type a web address, your browser sends a request to a computer somewhere and waits for the reply. A program on that computer has to be listening for those requests and answering them. That program is a **web server**, and NGINX (pronounced "engine x") is one of the most widely used.

NGINX has four jobs, and one site often uses several of them at once.

The simplest is serving **static files**: files sent exactly as they sit on disk, such as images, JavaScript and **HTML** files (the text files that describe a web page). NGINX finds the file and sends it, very fast.

Many sites build their pages with their own program, written in Python, JavaScript, Java and so on. That program is the **application server**, or **backend**. NGINX can stand in front of it as a **reverse proxy**: browsers only ever talk to NGINX, which passes each request on to the application and relays the answer back, like a receptionist forwarding calls.

When one copy of the application isn't enough, you run several copies, called **instances**. As a **load balancer**, NGINX spreads requests across them and stops sending traffic to a copy that has failed.

NGINX can also do the HTTPS work. It holds the certificate and does the scrambling that keeps traffic private (**encryption**), then talks plain HTTP to the applications behind it. This is called **TLS termination**.

Finally, it can keep a **cache**: stored copies of recent answers, so repeated requests don't reach the application at all.

Why is it so popular? NGINX can keep tens of thousands of connections open at once using only a handful of processes and little memory. Slow or idle visitors cost it almost nothing, so they don't tie up your application.

NGINX is free and **open source**: anyone may read, use and change its code. A paid edition, NGINX Plus, adds extras; this course uses the free one, which is what Linux distributions install.
concepts.code:
# One NGINX in front of everything
# browser --HTTPS--> NGINX
#                     |-- /       -> files in /var/www/site     (static files)
#                     |-- /api/   -> two copies of the app       (reverse proxy +
#                     |              on 10.0.0.11 and 10.0.0.12   load balancing)
#                     `-- /chat/  -> a separate chat service
curl -sI https://example.com | grep -i '^server'
# server: nginx          <- the response says which web server sent it
takeaways: NGINX serves files, passes requests to apps (reverse proxy), spreads load and handles HTTPS
Visitors talk only to NGINX; the applications sit behind it
A few NGINX processes can hold tens of thousands of connections cheaply

quiz.q: A site runs its app on three machines and wants NGINX to share visitors between them, skipping any machine that has crashed. Which NGINX job is that?
quiz.explain: Spreading requests across several copies of an app, and avoiding failed ones, is load balancing.

quiz.q: Browsers talk only to NGINX, which passes each request to a Python app and sends the app's answer back. What is NGINX acting as?
quiz.explain: A reverse proxy stands in front of the application and forwards requests to it.

concepts.name: Installing, testing and reloading
concepts.summary: Install NGINX, find its files, check the configuration with nginx -t and apply it with a graceful reload.
concepts.why: Knowing the test-then-reload routine prevents taking a site down with a typo.
concepts.body:
Install NGINX with your distribution's package manager (`sudo apt install nginx` on Debian or Ubuntu), or from nginx.org's own package repository when you need a newer version. The package also sets NGINX up to start with the machine. Typical file locations on Linux:

- `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf`: the main configuration file.
- `/etc/nginx/conf.d/*.conf` (and on Debian/Ubuntu `sites-enabled/`): one file per site, pulled in by the main file.
- `/var/log/nginx/access.log` and `error.log`: the logs.
- `/usr/share/nginx/html` or `/var/www/html`: the default welcome page.

The `nginx` command controls everything:

- `nginx -t`: test the configuration without touching the running server. It checks that every line follows NGINX's writing rules (its **syntax**) and that files it mentions exist. **Always run it before reloading.**
- `nginx -T`: test, then print the whole configuration with every included file pasted in. Great for finding where a setting really comes from.
- `nginx -s reload` (or `systemctl reload nginx`): apply a changed configuration with a graceful reload, explained below.
- `nginx -s quit` stops NGINX after current requests finish; `nginx -v` prints the version.

NGINX runs as one **master process**, which reads the configuration, plus a few **worker processes** that actually answer requests. "Process" here just means a running program.

On a **graceful reload** the master re-reads the configuration and starts fresh workers. The old workers finish the requests they're in the middle of, then exit. Visitors see no error and no connection is cut.

If the new configuration is broken, a reload keeps the old one running and writes the error to the error log. A full restart would stop NGINX and then fail to start it again, leaving no website at all. That's one more reason to prefer reload, and to test first.
concepts.code:
sudo apt install nginx
nginx -v                      # nginx version: nginx/1.30.6
sudo nginx -t
# nginx: the configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf syntax is ok
# nginx: configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf test is successful
sudo nginx -T | grep -n server_name      # search the full configuration
sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx   # reload only if the test passed
curl -sI http://localhost/ | head -2
# HTTP/1.1 200 OK
# Server: nginx/1.30.6
tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log           # watch new errors as they appear
takeaways: nginx -t tests the configuration; nginx -T tests and prints all of it
A reload is graceful: new workers start, old ones finish their requests first
Logs live in /var/log/nginx by default
pitfalls: Restarting instead of reloading: a broken config then leaves no server running.

quiz.q: You reload NGINX with a configuration that has a typo. What happens?
options: The old configuration keeps serving and the error is logged
NGINX returns an error page for every request
quiz.explain: The master process checks the new configuration first; if it's broken, the old workers simply keep running.

concepts.name: Configuration structure: directives and contexts
concepts.summary: Read nginx.conf: simple and block directives, the main, events, http, server and location contexts, includes and inheritance.
concepts.why: Every NGINX feature is a directive in some context; knowing the structure tells you where each line belongs.
concepts.body:
An NGINX configuration file is a list of settings called **directives**. A simple directive is a name, one or more values and a semicolon: `worker_processes auto;`.

A **block directive** holds other directives inside braces `{ }`. That block is called a **context**, because it decides where the directives inside it apply. The main ones, from the outside in:

- **main**: the top level, outside any braces. Settings for NGINX's own processes, such as `user` and `worker_processes`.
- `events { }`: how NGINX handles connections, such as `worker_connections`.
- `http { }`: everything about web traffic: file types, logging, compression and the sites themselves.
- `server { }`: one website, chosen by the address in its `listen` and its `server_name`.
- `location { }`: settings for some of the paths of a site, such as everything under `/images/`.
- `upstream { }`: a named group of application servers to pass requests to (inside `http`).
- `stream { }`: forwarding non-web traffic, such as database connections; separate from `http`.

In `https://example.com/images/cat.png?size=2`, the part after the site name, `/images/cat.png?size=2`, is what NGINX calls the **URI**. `location` blocks pick requests by its path.

Each directive is allowed only in certain contexts; its documentation lists them.

Settings flow downwards, which NGINX calls **inheritance**: a directive set in `http` applies to every `server` and `location` inside it, unless one of them sets its own value, which then wins there.

One rule surprises everyone. A few directives can be repeated to build a list, such as `add_header` (each one adds a header to responses). Such a list is inherited **only if the inner block has none of its own**. Adding a single `add_header` in a location silently drops every header set at the server level.

`include` pulls in other files and accepts wildcards like `*.conf`, which is how each site gets its own file. Comments start with `#`.
takeaways: Directives end with ;, blocks create contexts
main > events / http > server > location
Inner contexts inherit settings, but add_header-like lists are replaced if redefined
pitfalls: Adding one add_header in a location and losing all server-level security headers.

quiz.q: The server block sets two add_header lines; a location inside it sets one different add_header. Which headers does that location send?
quiz.explain: add_header is inherited only when the current level defines no add_header of its own.

concepts.name: Server blocks: listen and server_name
concepts.summary: Run several sites on one NGINX with server blocks, and see how a request is matched by port, name and default_server.
concepts.why: Picking the wrong server block is the classic reason a site shows another site's content.
concepts.body:
One NGINX can serve many websites. Each site gets its own `server` block, also called a **virtual server**. To pick one, NGINX uses two network ideas.

Every machine on a network has a numeric **IP address**, like `203.0.113.7`, the way every house has a street address. And one machine runs many network programs, so each listens on a numbered **port**, like flats in one building: plain HTTP normally uses port 80 and HTTPS port 443.

Every request also carries a **Host header** naming the site the browser asked for, such as `www.example.com`. That's how many sites can share one IP address.

NGINX chooses a server block for each request in two steps:

- First by **address and port**: only servers whose `listen` matches where the connection arrived are candidates.
- Then by the Host header, compared with `server_name`.

`server_name` accepts several forms, checked in this priority order:

- exact names: `example.com www.example.com`
- the longest wildcard starting with `*`: `*.example.com`
- the longest wildcard ending with `*`: `mail.*`
- the first matching regular expression, in file order: `~^(?<sub>.+)\.example\.com$`

If no name matches, the request goes to the **default server** for that address and port: the one marked `listen 80 default_server`, or otherwise simply the first server block defined for it. That's why requests for unknown names, or for a bare IP address, sometimes land on a random site.

A good practice is an explicit catch-all that rejects unknown names. `return 444` is an NGINX-only code that closes the connection without sending anything.

The special name `.example.com` matches both `example.com` and every **subdomain** of it (names like `shop.example.com` under it).
takeaways: Servers are matched by listen address/port, then by server_name
Exact names beat wildcards, which beat regexes
No match goes to default_server, or the first server for that port
pitfalls: Relying on file order for the default server; mark it explicitly with default_server.

quiz.q: No server_name matches the Host header and no server is marked default_server. Which block handles the request?
options: The first server block listening on that address and port
quiz.explain: Without an explicit default_server, the first server block for that address and port is the default.

concepts.name: Static files: root, alias and try_files
concepts.summary: Map URLs to files with root and alias, choose index files, and use try_files for fallbacks such as single-page apps.
concepts.why: Serving a website's built files and images from NGINX is fast and common, and root vs alias mistakes cause most 404s.
concepts.body:
`root` names the folder NGINX looks in, and the **whole URI** is added to its end: with `root /var/www/site;`, a request for `/img/logo.png` reads `/var/www/site/img/logo.png`.

`alias` **replaces** the part matched by the location instead: in `location /static/ { alias /srv/assets/; }`, `/static/app.js` reads `/srv/assets/app.js`. Keep the trailing slashes the same on both, or paths get glued together wrongly.

`index index.html;` sets the **index** file: the file served when a request asks for a folder (a URI ending in `/`).

`try_files` checks alternatives in order and uses the first that exists; the last item is a fallback URI (or `=404`):

- `try_files $uri $uri/ =404;`: the file, then a folder with an index file, otherwise 404.
- `try_files $uri /index.html;`: the classic setup for a **single-page application**.

A single-page application is a site that loads one HTML page once, then redraws it with JavaScript as you click. Its addresses like `/settings` aren't real files, so unknown paths get `index.html`, and the app's JavaScript shows the right screen.

Other useful directives for static files:

- `expires 30d;` or `add_header Cache-Control ...` tells browsers to cache a file instead of downloading it again. Long times are safe for files whose name changes whenever their content does, like `app.3f9a1c.js`.
- `autoindex on;` shows a listing of a folder's files (rarely wanted on a live site).
- File types come from `mime.types`; a wrong `Content-Type` usually means it isn't included.

NGINX uses the `sendfile` system call, which asks the kernel to send a file straight to the network without NGINX copying it first. That makes static serving very cheap.
takeaways: root appends the full URI; alias replaces the location prefix
try_files tries files in order, then falls back
try_files $uri /index.html serves single-page apps
pitfalls: Using root where alias was meant: /downloads/a.zip becomes /srv/files/downloads/a.zip.

quiz.q: With location /img/ { root /data; }, which file serves /img/a.png?
quiz.explain: root appends the whole URI, including the /img/ prefix.

concepts.name: How location blocks are matched
concepts.summary: Learn the exact order NGINX uses to pick a location: exact match, longest prefix, ^~, then regular expressions in file order.
concepts.why: Most confusing NGINX behaviour comes from a different location matching than the one you expected.
concepts.body:
A server usually contains several **location blocks**, and **exactly one** handles each request. The modifiers are:

- `location = /path`: exact match.
- `location /prefix`: prefix match.
- `location ^~ /prefix`: prefix match that, if it is the longest, disables regex checking.
- `location ~ regex` (case-sensitive) and `location ~* regex` (case-insensitive).

The steps NGINX follows, which do **not** simply follow file order:

- If an `=` location matches exactly, use it and stop.
- Find the **longest matching prefix** location and remember it. If it has `^~`, use it and stop.
- Check regular expression locations **in the order they appear**; the first match wins.
- If no regex matches, use the remembered longest prefix.

So a regex like `~ \.php$` beats the prefix `/uploads/` for `/uploads/x.php`, unless that prefix is written `^~ /uploads/`. Order matters only among regexes.

Matching uses the URI's path after cleaning it up (for example `%20` becomes a space), without the query string. Locations can be nested, and named locations (`location @fallback`) are used only as targets of `try_files` or `error_page`, never matched directly.
takeaways: = exact wins immediately; ^~ longest prefix skips regexes
Otherwise the first matching regex in file order beats prefixes
Only one location handles a request
pitfalls: Expecting the longest prefix to win over a regex; regexes are checked after prefixes and win if they match.

options: Whichever comes first in the file
quiz.explain: After remembering the longest prefix, NGINX checks regexes; a matching regex wins unless the prefix used ^~.

concepts.name: Reverse proxy with proxy_pass
concepts.summary: Forward requests to an application server with proxy_pass, pass the right headers, and get the trailing-slash URI rules right.
concepts.why: Putting NGINX in front of an application is the most common NGINX job, and header or path mistakes break apps subtly.
concepts.body:
`proxy_pass` forwards a request to a backend and returns its response. NGINX calls the servers behind it **upstream**, and the URI it sends upstream follows a precise rule:

- **Without a URI part** (`proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000;`) the original request URI is passed unchanged: `/api/users` stays `/api/users`.
- **With a URI part**, even just `/` (`proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000/;`), the part matching the location prefix is **replaced** by it: in `location /api/`, `/api/users` becomes `/users`.

By default NGINX sends `Host` as the upstream address and adds nothing about the client, so the app sees NGINX as the client. Pass the original information explicitly:

- `proxy_set_header Host $host;`
- `proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;`
- `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;`
- `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;` so apps generate `https` URLs.

The application must be configured to trust these headers only when they come from NGINX.

**Timeouts** set how long NGINX waits before giving up: `proxy_connect_timeout` for connecting, `proxy_read_timeout` (default 60s) for the answer. When the backend is down or too slow, the client gets a **502** or **504**. Upstream errors and their reasons appear in the error log.
takeaways: proxy_pass without URI keeps the path; with a URI it replaces the location prefix
Forward the Host header, X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto explicitly
502 = backend unreachable, 504 = backend timeout
pitfalls: Adding or forgetting a trailing slash in proxy_pass and getting doubled or missing path prefixes.

quiz.q: In location /app/ { proxy_pass http://b:3000/; }, what path does the backend see for /app/login?
quiz.explain: With a URI in proxy_pass, the matched prefix /app/ is replaced by /.

concepts.name: Access and error logs
concepts.summary: Configure access_log and error_log, define log formats including JSON and upstream timings, and read logs to track down problems.
concepts.why: Logs are the first place to look for every 4xx, 5xx or slow request, and custom formats make them far more useful.
concepts.body:
NGINX writes two logs.

The **error log** (`error_log path level;`) records problems: missing files, upstream failures, configuration warnings. Levels go from `debug` through `info`, `notice`, `warn`, `error` up to `emerg`; the default is `error`. Upstream errors show the exact cause, such as `connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream`.

The **access log** records every request using a **log_format**. The predefined `combined` format contains client address, time, request line, status code, body size, the page the visitor came from (the referer) and the browser's own name for itself (the user agent). Define your own with variables:

- `$request_time`: total time NGINX spent on the request.
- `$upstream_response_time`, `$upstream_addr`, `$upstream_status`: what the backend did; essential for finding slow requests.
- `$request_id`: a unique ID you can also pass to the backend as a header, to match its log lines with NGINX's.

`log_format name escape=json '{...}'` writes each line as JSON, which log-collecting tools read directly, no regular expressions needed.

`access_log off;` turns logging off for noisy locations, such as a **health check** URL that monitoring tools call every few seconds to ask "are you alive?".

`access_log ... buffer=32k flush=5s;` writes to disk in batches on busy servers, and adding `if=$loggable` logs only requests where that variable isn't empty or 0. The official Docker setup sends both logs to standard output and standard error instead of files.
takeaways: error_log for problems, access_log for every request
Log $request_time and $upstream_response_time to find slowness
escape=json gives machine-readable logs
pitfalls: Investigating 502 errors from the access log alone; the error log says why the upstream failed.

quiz.q: A request took 3 s according to $request_time but $upstream_response_time is 2.9 s. Where is the time spent?
quiz.explain: Upstream response time measures the backend; it accounts for almost all of the total.

concepts.name: HTTPS and TLS termination
concepts.summary: Serve HTTPS with certificates, enable HTTP/2, redirect HTTP to HTTPS and choose sane TLS settings.
concepts.why: Every public site must use HTTPS, and NGINX is usually where TLS is terminated.
concepts.body:
A TLS server needs `listen 443 ssl;`, a certificate and its **private key** (the secret file that proves the certificate is yours). Browsers trust your certificate through a **certificate chain**: your site's certificate plus the in-between (intermediate) certificates that link it to an authority they already trust. Two directives set them up:

- `ssl_certificate` must contain the server certificate **followed by intermediate certificates** (a "fullchain" file). Missing intermediates work in some browsers and fail in others and in curl.
- `ssl_certificate_key` is the private key; keep it readable only by root.

**HTTP/2** is a newer version of HTTP that carries many requests at once over one connection. Since NGINX 1.25.1 you turn it on with `http2 on;`; the old `http2` flag on `listen` is **deprecated** (still accepted, but going away). HTTP/3 uses `listen 443 quic;` and needs NGINX built with QUIC support.

Recommended settings:

- `ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;` (the modern default).
- `ssl_session_cache shared:SSL:10m;` so returning visitors can skip most of the TLS setup.
- An `add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000" always;` header (**HSTS**: it tells browsers to use only HTTPS for your site for a year) once you are sure HTTPS works everywhere.

Redirect plain HTTP with a small server: `return 301 https://$host$request_uri;`. Keep a `location /.well-known/acme-challenge/` on port 80 if you use **Let's Encrypt**, a free service that issues certificates and proves you own the site by fetching a file from there; `certbot` can edit NGINX configuration and renew certificates automatically, after which NGINX needs a reload to pick up the new files.

Test with `curl -vI https://...` and a free online checker such as SSL Labs.
takeaways: listen 443 ssl plus a fullchain certificate and key
`http2 on;` enables HTTP/2 since 1.25.1
Redirect port 80 with `return 301 https://$host$request_uri`
pitfalls: Configuring only the leaf certificate without intermediates; some clients then fail verification.

quiz.q: Browsers accept your site but curl reports 'unable to get local issuer certificate'. Most likely cause?
quiz.explain: Browsers may fetch or cache intermediates; curl needs the server to send the full chain.

concepts.name: Redirects, rewrites and variables
concepts.summary: Redirect with return, rewrite URIs with regex captures, and use built-in variables like `$host`, `$uri` and `$args`.
concepts.why: Site migrations, canonical domains and clean URLs all need redirects, and return is simpler and safer than rewrite.
concepts.body:
`return` stops processing and sends a response:

- `return 301 https://example.com$request_uri;`: permanent redirect (308 also keeps the HTTP method and body).
- `return 302 /maintenance.html;`: temporary redirect.
- `return 403;` or `return 200 "ok";` for a direct response.

`rewrite regex replacement [flag];` changes the URI using regex captures:

- With no flag, NGINX continues with the next rewrite and then re-searches locations for the new URI.
- `last`: stop rewrites here and search locations again with the new URI.
- `break`: stop rewrites and keep processing in the current location.
- `redirect` (302) and `permanent` (301): send a redirect to the client. A replacement starting with `http://` or `https://` also redirects.

Prefer `return` whenever the target doesn't need a regex; it is clearer and cheaper.

Common variables: `$host` (Host header or server name), `$request_uri` (original URI with query string), `$uri` (normalized, possibly rewritten, without query string), `$args` and `$arg_name` for the query string, `$scheme`, `$remote_addr` and `$http_<header>` for any request header.

The `map` directive computes one variable from another and is the clean way to handle many redirects: keep a table of old to new paths instead of dozens of rewrites.
takeaways: return for redirects and direct responses; rewrite only when you need regexes
last re-searches locations; break stays in the current one
`$request_uri` keeps the query string; `$uri` doesn't
pitfalls: Redirecting with $uri instead of $request_uri and losing the query string.

quiz.q: Which variable keeps the original path and query string for a redirect?
quiz.explain: $request_uri is the original request URI including arguments; $uri is the normalized path only.

concepts.name: Load balancing with upstream
concepts.summary: Spread traffic across backends with upstream groups, choose a balancing strategy, and handle failures and kept-open connections.
concepts.why: Running more than one application instance needs a balancer that also routes around failures.
concepts.body:
An `upstream` block names a group of servers; `proxy_pass http://name;` sends requests to it.

Balancing strategies:

- **round robin** (default): each server in turn, optionally with `weight=` to give some more.
- `least_conn;`: the server with the fewest open connections; good when some requests take much longer than others.
- `ip_hash;` or `hash $key consistent;`: always send the same client (or key) to the same server.
- `random two least_conn;`: pick two at random, take the less busy.

NGINX does **passive health checks**: it notices failures in real traffic rather than testing servers itself. With `max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s`, a server that fails 3 times within 30 seconds is skipped for 30 seconds.

`proxy_next_upstream` decides what counts as a failure (by default `error timeout`) and whether the request is **retried**, meaning tried again on the next server. Requests that aren't safe to repeat, like a POST that might charge a card twice, are only retried if you explicitly allow it. A server marked `backup` gets traffic only when all the others are down. Checks that actively send test requests are a feature of the paid NGINX Plus.

**Keepalive** to upstreams reuses open connections to the backends instead of opening a new one for every request. Add `keepalive 32;` to the upstream, plus `proxy_http_version 1.1;` and `proxy_set_header Connection "";` in the location. Without those two, NGINX talks HTTP/1.0 to the backends and closes the connection after every request.
takeaways: upstream groups servers; round robin by default, least_conn and hash available
max_fails/fail_timeout are passive health checks; a spare server marked `backup` only gets traffic when the rest are down
Upstream keepalive needs HTTP/1.1 and an empty Connection header
pitfalls: Adding keepalive in upstream but not proxy_http_version 1.1, so connections are still closed.

quiz.q: Which method keeps sending the same client IP to the same backend?
quiz.explain: ip_hash maps clients by address to a consistent server.

concepts.name: Access control and security headers
concepts.summary: Restrict locations by IP with allow/deny, add basic authentication, set security headers and hide version details.
concepts.why: Admin panels, monitoring pages and test copies of a site need protection at the edge, and headers harden every page.
concepts.body:
NGINX has several simple access controls:

- `allow` and `deny` check the client's IP address in order; the first match wins. End with `deny all;`.
- `auth_basic "Restricted";` with `auth_basic_user_file` makes the browser ask for a username and password, checked against an **htpasswd file** (create it with `htpasswd` from apache2-utils, or `openssl passwd`). Use it only over HTTPS, since the password is sent with every request.
- `satisfy any;` lets in either an allowed address or a valid password; the default `satisfy all` requires both.

`auth_request /auth;` hands the decision to another service. For each request NGINX first makes a small internal request (a **subrequest**) to your login service and lets the visitor through only if that answers 2xx. This is how a company-wide login (single sign-on) is put in front of apps that have none.

Some response headers make browsers safer. Add them with `add_header ... always;` so they appear on error pages too:

- `Strict-Transport-Security` (HSTS), `X-Content-Type-Options nosniff`, `Content-Security-Policy` (which sources a page may load) and `Referrer-Policy`.
- `X-Frame-Options` or CSP `frame-ancestors` against **clickjacking**: another site showing yours in an invisible frame to trick people into clicking.

`server_tokens off;` removes the version number from the `Server` header and error pages. Remember the `add_header` inheritance rule: put shared headers in an included snippet and include it wherever a location adds its own headers.

Also limit request size with `client_max_body_size` (default 1m) so uploads can't fill the disk.
takeaways: allow/deny are checked in order; finish with deny all
auth_basic needs HTTPS; satisfy any combines IP and password
Add security headers with always; server_tokens off hides the version
pitfalls: Forgetting always on add_header, so headers are missing from 4xx and 5xx responses.

quiz.q: With satisfy any, allow 10.0.0.0/8, deny all and auth_basic, who gets in?
options: Only internal IPs with a password
Internal IPs, or anyone with valid credentials
quiz.explain: satisfy any grants access if either the IP rules or the password check allows it.

concepts.name: Proxy caching
concepts.summary: Cache backend responses with proxy_cache_path and proxy_cache, control validity, serve old copies when the backend fails, and check the cache status.
concepts.why: A well-configured cache can absorb most traffic and keep a site up while the backend is struggling.
concepts.body:
Caching the backend's responses takes two pieces:

- `proxy_cache_path` (in `http`) defines the storage: a directory, `levels` for subdirectories, a **keys_zone**: memory shared by all workers that lists what is cached (1 MB holds about 8,000 entries), `max_size` and `inactive` (remove items not accessed for that long).
- `proxy_cache zone_name;` in a server or location enables it.

What gets cached and for how long:

- By default NGINX respects the backend's `Cache-Control`, `Expires` and `Set-Cookie` headers; responses with `Set-Cookie` or `private`/`no-store` are not cached.
- `proxy_cache_valid 200 301 10m;` sets lifetimes when the backend gives none.
- `proxy_cache_key` defaults to `$scheme$proxy_host$request_uri`; add cookies or headers carefully if responses vary by them.
- Only GET and HEAD are cached by default.

Resilience features:

- `proxy_cache_use_stale error timeout updating http_500 http_502 http_503 http_504;` serves expired ("stale") copies when the backend fails.
- `proxy_cache_background_update on;` refreshes stale items in the background.
- `proxy_cache_lock on;` lets only one request fetch a missing item while the others wait, avoiding a **cache stampede** (hundreds of requests hitting the backend for the same thing at once).

Add `add_header X-Cache-Status $upstream_cache_status;` to see `MISS`, `HIT`, `EXPIRED`, `STALE` or `BYPASS` while testing.
takeaways: proxy_cache_path defines storage; proxy_cache enables it per location
use_stale and background_update keep serving when the backend fails
$upstream_cache_status shows HIT, MISS, STALE and more
pitfalls: Caching personalised pages under a shared key; bypass the cache for logged-in users or vary the key.

quiz.q: The backend is down but an expired copy exists. Which directive lets NGINX return it?
quiz.explain: proxy_cache_use_stale lists the conditions under which stale content may be served.

concepts.name: Rate and connection limiting
concepts.summary: Limit how fast clients may send requests with limit_req_zone and limit_req, understand burst and nodelay, and cap open connections.
concepts.why: Rate limits protect login pages and APIs from abuse and keep one client from starving the others.
concepts.body:
A **rate limit** caps how many requests one client may make per second or minute. NGINX's works like a **leaky bucket**: requests pour in at any speed but drain out at a fixed rate, and when the bucket is full, extra requests are turned away.

`limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=api:10m rate=10r/s;` (in `http`) defines a shared zone keyed by client address. `$binary_remote_addr` is compact: a 10 MB zone tracks around 160,000 addresses. The key can be any variable, such as an API key header.

`limit_req zone=api;` in a location applies it. Without other options, requests arriving faster than the rate (here one per 100 ms) are **rejected immediately**, even short bursts. Two options fix that:

- `burst=20`: queue up to 20 excess requests; they are released at the configured rate, so they are delayed.
- `nodelay`: process queued burst requests immediately, while still counting them; requests beyond the burst are rejected. This is usually what APIs want: bursts are allowed, sustained abuse is not.
- `delay=8` (instead of nodelay): first 8 excess requests go without delay, the rest are delayed.

Rejected requests get `503` by default; set `limit_req_status 429;` for the correct "Too Many Requests". `limit_req_dry_run on;` logs what would be limited without enforcing it, ideal for tuning.

`limit_conn_zone` and `limit_conn` cap the number of connections **open at the same time** per key, for example to stop one client from opening hundreds of downloads.
takeaways: limit_req_zone defines key, size and rate; limit_req applies it
burst queues excess; nodelay serves the burst at once
Use limit_req_status 429 and dry-run mode while tuning
pitfalls: Rate limiting by $remote_addr behind a load balancer: every client shares the balancer's IP; set up `real_ip` first so NGINX reads the client's address from the balancer's header.

quiz.q: rate=10r/s with burst=20 nodelay. A client sends 25 requests at once. What happens?
options: 21 are served immediately and 4 are rejected
quiz.explain: One request fits the rate plus 20 burst slots served without delay; the remaining 4 exceed the burst.

concepts.name: WebSockets, timeouts and buffering
concepts.summary: Pass WebSockets and other long-lived connections through NGINX, tune timeouts, and know when to turn proxy buffering off.
concepts.why: Real-time features and streaming responses break behind NGINX's default settings.
concepts.body:
A **WebSocket** is a connection that stays open so browser and server can both send messages at any time, as chat and live updates need. It starts as an HTTP request with `Upgrade: websocket` and `Connection: Upgrade`. These are **hop-by-hop headers**, meant for one connection only, so NGINX doesn't pass them on unless told to. You need HTTP/1.1 to the backend and the two headers set explicitly. A `map` makes `Connection` correct for both WebSocket and normal requests.

**Timeouts**: `proxy_read_timeout` (default 60s) is the maximum time between two reads from the backend. An idle WebSocket, or a long-polling request (one the server holds open until it has news), is closed after it, so raise it for those locations, or have the application send pings. `proxy_send_timeout` is the write equivalent; `proxy_connect_timeout` limits connection setup.

**Proxy buffering**: by default NGINX first reads the backend's whole response into memory (or temporary files if large), then sends it to the client. That frees the backend quickly even for slow clients, which is usually what you want. But it delays **streaming** responses that should arrive bit by bit: **server-sent events** (one response that keeps delivering updates), AI chat answers written out word by word, or progress output. Options:

- `proxy_buffering off;` in that location.
- The backend can send `X-Accel-Buffering: no` for individual responses.

Request bodies are also buffered fully by default; `proxy_request_buffering off;` streams uploads directly to the backend.
takeaways: WebSockets need proxy_http_version 1.1 plus Upgrade and Connection headers
proxy_read_timeout closes idle upstream connections (60s default)
Turn proxy_buffering off for streaming responses
pitfalls: WebSocket connections dropping every 60 seconds because proxy_read_timeout was left at the default.

quiz.q: A streaming endpoint delivers all its output at once at the end, only when behind NGINX. Likely fix?
quiz.explain: Proxy buffering collects the response before sending it; disabling it streams data as it arrives.

concepts.name: Master, workers and the event loop
concepts.summary: How the master and worker processes divide work, how many connections NGINX can hold, and what really happens during reload and upgrade.
concepts.why: Capacity planning, file descriptor limits and zero-downtime operations all follow from the process model.
concepts.body:
NGINX runs one **master process** as root, so it can open ports below 1024 and read certificates, and several **worker processes** as an unprivileged user, which handle all traffic. Optional cache manager and cache loader processes look after the disk cache.

`worker_processes auto;` starts one worker per CPU core. Each worker is a single thread running an **event loop**: it asks the kernel (through `epoll` on Linux, `kqueue` on BSD and macOS) which of its many connections have data ready, handles those, and asks again. It never sits waiting on one slow connection.

`worker_connections` caps open connections **per worker**, counting both client and upstream connections. So an NGINX that forwards every request, with 4 workers and 1024 connections each handles about 2,000 clients whose requests go to a backend, not 4,096.

Each connection uses a file descriptor (the kernel's handle for an open file or connection), so raise `worker_rlimit_nofile` and the system limits to match.

Reading from a slow disk can still stall a worker, because the kernel makes it wait (the read is **blocking**). `aio threads` hands those reads to a thread pool, a few helper threads.

By default the kernel wakes workers to accept new connections; `listen ... reuseport` gives each worker its own listening socket so the kernel spreads connections evenly.

On **reload** (signal SIGHUP) the master checks the new configuration, opens new sockets if needed, starts new workers and tells old ones to stop. Old workers stop accepting and finish their current requests, which for long WebSockets can take a long time (`worker_shutdown_timeout` caps it). A **live upgrade** (SIGUSR2) starts a new master from a new NGINX program file alongside the old one, so even upgrades lose no connections.
takeaways: Master (root) manages; workers (unprivileged) run event loops
worker_connections counts client and upstream connections per worker
Reload starts new workers and lets old ones finish; SIGUSR2 swaps in a new NGINX program live
pitfalls: Sizing capacity as workers x worker_connections clients when NGINX forwards every request; each forwarded request uses two connections.

quiz.q: 4 workers, worker_connections 1024, every request proxied upstream. Roughly how many concurrent clients?
quiz.explain: Each proxied client uses one client and one upstream connection, halving capacity.

concepts.name: Request phases, if and map
concepts.summary: Follow a request through NGINX's processing phases and understand why if inside location is dangerous and map is preferred.
concepts.why: Phase order explains why directives that look sequential aren't, and avoids the infamous if pitfalls.
concepts.body:
NGINX configuration is **declarative**: it describes what you want, not steps to run from top to bottom. Each request passes through fixed **request phases**, and each directive runs in the phase its feature belongs to, regardless of the order you wrote them:

- `server_rewrite` (rewrite directives at server level), `find_config` (choose the location), `rewrite` (rewrite directives in the location), `post_rewrite` (restart location search if the URI changed),
- `preaccess` (limit_req, limit_conn), `access` (allow/deny, auth_basic, auth_request), `post_access` (`satisfy`),
- `precontent` (`try_files`), `content` (proxy_pass, static files, `return` is actually in rewrite), and `log`.

So `return` runs in the rewrite phase, before `allow`/`deny`: a `return 200` in a location is served even to denied clients.

`if` is part of the rewrite feature. Inside a `location`, a true `if` creates a hidden nested location and the request is handled by **that** configuration, which inherits some directives and silently drops others such as `try_files`. The only fully safe things inside `if` in a location are `return` and `rewrite ... last`.

**`map`** is the idiomatic alternative: it defines a variable computed from others, worked out only when something actually reads it, so unused maps cost nothing. Variables like `$limit_key` from a map can then feed limit zones, logging conditions or headers sent to the backend, without any `if`.
takeaways: Directives run in their phase, not in file order
return and rewrite run before access checks
Inside location, use if only for return or rewrite ... last; prefer map
pitfalls: Putting proxy_pass or try_files logic inside if blocks and getting inexplicable behaviour.

quiz.q: A location contains deny all; and return 200 "ok";. What does a client get?
options: 200 ok, because return runs in the rewrite phase before access
quiz.explain: The rewrite phase, where return executes, comes before the access phase.

concepts.name: Tuning compression, files and keepalive
concepts.summary: Tune gzip, sendfile, open_file_cache, keepalive and buffers, and know which settings actually matter.
concepts.why: Default settings are conservative; a few targeted changes give large gains, while cargo-cult tuning wastes time.
concepts.body:
Start by measuring (`$request_time`, `$upstream_response_time`, a load-testing tool). Then the settings that usually matter:

**Compression**: `gzip on;` with `gzip_types` for text formats (HTML is always included) and `gzip_min_length 1024`. Level 4 to 6 is the sweet spot; higher costs CPU for little gain. Don't gzip images or video, which are already compressed. `gzip_static on;` serves precompressed `.gz` files from the build, costing no CPU. Brotli, a newer and smaller compression format, needs an extra **module** built by others and compiled into NGINX.

**Static files**: `sendfile on;` sends file data inside the kernel; `tcp_nopush on;` sends headers and the file start together; `tcp_nodelay on;` (default) avoids delays for small keepalive writes. `open_file_cache max=10000 inactive=30s;` remembers open files and their details (size, date) for sites with many small files.

**Connections**: client `keepalive_timeout` (default 75s) and `keepalive_requests` (default 1000) control how long and how often a browser's connection is reused. Upstream `keepalive` saves setting up a new connection to the backends for each request, often the biggest win when NGINX forwards most traffic. Reusing TLS setups (`ssl_session_cache`) and HTTP/2 cut down on TLS **handshakes**, the opening exchange that sets up encryption.

**Buffers**: `proxy_buffers` and `proxy_buffer_size` sized for typical responses avoid writing to temp files; the error log warns "an upstream response is buffered to a temporary file" when they're too small. `client_body_buffer_size` does the same for uploads.
takeaways: gzip text at level 4-6; gzip_static serves prebuilt .gz files
sendfile, tcp_nopush and open_file_cache speed static serving
Upstream keepalive and buffer sizing matter most when NGINX forwards to backends
pitfalls: Gzipping already-compressed images, burning CPU for no size gain.

quiz.q: The error log keeps saying an upstream response is buffered to a temporary file. What should you consider?
quiz.explain: Responses larger than the memory buffers spill to disk; bigger buffers keep them in memory.
